title: Responder Toolkit: Rapid Stabilization Recipes and Customer Commitment Matrix
author: Sofia Chen
body:
Summary
This document is a compact, operations-focused toolkit for first-responders and bridge operators at Redwood Inference. It combines: 1) short, repeatable stabilization recipes for common failure modes; 2) a customer-commitment matrix that maps incident classes to status cadence and escalation steps; 3) ready-to-send status page and customer communication templates; and 4) a lightweight game-day syllabus for validating the runloop. The content is deliberately actionable and intended to be copied into runbooks and incident bridges.

Scope
- Audience: on-call engineers, SRE bridge operators, support escalation leads, and on-call managers.
- Services in scope: API Gateway (redwood-api), Serving runtime (redwood-runtime), KV cache layer (kv-cache), Ingress proxy (edge-proxy), and Observability pipeline (obs-collector).
- Out of scope: long-term remediation plans and product feature change requests (those belong in the follow-up postmortem and product board).

Ownership and roles
- Primary responder: the on-call engineer assigned to the affected service. Responsible for immediate triage and mitigation.
- Bridge operator: coordinates cross-team actions, owns external comms until Customer Success takes over.
- Escalation owner: team's tech lead / service owner. Approves scaling or rollback actions.
- Communications lead: Customer Success for customer-facing email/phone.

Incident classification and customer-commitment matrix
(Use this table as a decision matrix when deciding cadence and escalation.)
- Sev 1 (Service down / >90% customers impacted): Immediate bridge, hourly public status updates, exec notification, SLA credit review.
- Sev 2 (Partial outage / 10–90% impacted or severe SLO regression): Bridge within 15 min, 2-hour customer cadence until stable, product owner looped.
- Sev 3 (Degraded performance / <10% impact, latency SLO slip): Triage on-call leads bridge if not recovered in 1 hour, status page internal note; scheduled customer notice if persistent >24h.
- Sev 4 (Minor / cosmetic / internal alerts): Track in ticket, no external comm required unless escalated.

Quick triage ladder (first 10 minutes)
1) Acknowledge: Hit the alert, accept the pager, open the team channel and create a bridge. Post initial one-liner: "acknowledged — gathering evidence (service, region, brief symptom)".
2) Scope: Verify whether the issue is regional, model-specific, or platform-wide. Run the following probes:
   - curl -sS https://redwood-api.internal/health | jq .status
   - kubectl get pods -n runtime -l app=redwood-runtime --field-selector=status.phase!=Running
   - PromQL quick checks (Grafana Explore):
       * rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count[5m]) by (job)
       * sum(rate(redis_commands_total[2m])) by (instance)
3) Mitigate: Apply a safe, reversible mitigation with clear owner and ETA (examples below).
4) Communicate: Update the bridge with the current hypothesis and the mitigation being tried. Post to #alerts and notify Customer Success if impact >= Sev 2.

Stabilization recipes (concise, reversible actions)
- Latency spike (sudden increase in p95):
  1) Hypothesis checklist: noisy neighbor, sudden larger inputs, KV cache miss storm, model cache eviction.
  2) Quick actions: increase replica count by +1 for the runtime pool in the affected region; enable conservative throttling at the gateway.
     - kubectl scale deployment/redwood-runtime --replicas=$(($(kubectl get deploy redwood-runtime -o jsonpath='{.status.replicas}')+1)) -n runtime
     - Proxy config: curl -X PATCH https://edge-proxy.internal/config -d '{"global_rate_limit": "80%"}'
  3) Observe 2x token/sec and p95 over 10 minutes; rollback scale if no benefit.

- KV cache eviction storm (cache miss flood):
  1) Symptoms: cache hit ratio falls from ~98% to <85%; backend fetch latency increases.
  2) Actions: temporarily disable cache pre-warming, reduce cache TTLs for non-critical keys, enable emergency cache bypass for heavy keys.
  3) Command: redis-cli -h kv-cache.internal INFO keyspace | head -n 2
  4) Follow-up: schedule defensive quantile-based cache admission policy in the next retro.

- Model quality regression (sudden rise in hallucinations or quality alerts):
  1) If automated evals detect regression: switch traffic to last-known-good model variant (pin model version) via routing policy.
     - Example: POST /routing/api/v1/traffic -d '{"model":"rw-13b-v1","traffic":100}'
  2) If model is managed by provider, enable auto-fallback to verified smaller variant and open model-onboarding ticket.

- Capacity saturation (GPUs at 95%+ queue depth):
  1) Actions: enable burst capacity pool, re-route non-critical tenants to lower-tier model; temporarily raise batching timeout threshold to reduce context-switching.
  2) Command (internal): /ops/tools/capacity --activate-burst --pool=dedicated-burst-01 --region=us-west-2

- Observability pipeline outage (logs/metrics delayed):
  1) Symptom: gaps in metrics; alerts may be false negatives.
  2) Actions: promote a historical snapshot view for the bridge, continue incident handling using API telemetry and trace samples. Contact obs-team and escalate if >30m.

Evidence checklist (minimum artifacts to capture during incident)
- Timestamped incident start/ack times (ISO 8601).
- Alert payloads and IDs (full JSON).
- Representative request traces (trace IDs) and slow query samples.
- Relevant logs (service logs, proxy logs, redis logs) clipped to time window +/- 30m.
- Metrics charts (PNG or link) showing SLO breach window.
- Commands run and actions taken (who ran them).

Communications: templates and cadence
- Status page short (initial):
  Title: Service Latency Degradation — Investigating
  Impact: Some customers in us-west-2 may experience slower responses.
  ETA: Next update in 60 minutes.
  Body: "We are investigating increased request latency impacting a subset of customers. Engineers are actively triaging and mitigating. We will post a next update in 60 minutes or sooner if there is a substantive change."

- Status page long (when more detail available):
  Title: API Gateway Degraded — KV cache miss storm
  Impact: ~18% of requests in us-west-2 see >500ms additional latency.
  Root cause (hypothesis): Sudden cache miss storm caused by automated workload spike.
  Mitigation: Temporarily reduced TTLs, scaled runtime replicas, and enabled conservative rate limiting at the edge.
  Next update: in 2 hours or upon stabilization.

- Customer email (for Sev 1 / 2 initial notice):
  Subject: Redwood Inference — Partial Service Impact in us-west-2
  Body: "Hello — We are experiencing a partial service disruption affecting inference latency for some requests in us-west-2. Our engineers have opened an incident and are actively working to restore normal performance. We will provide hourly updates via status.redwood.com and a follow-up post-incident analysis. If you have an active incident with customer impact, reply to this message and our support team will prioritize a customer liaison call."

- Slack bridge templates (one-liners to copy into channel):
  - Initial: "[ACK] Investigating increased p95 latency for redwood-runtime (us-west-2). Bridge: <bridge-link>. Primary: @alice. Hypothesis: cache miss storm."
  - Mitigation applied: "Mitigation: scaled runtime by +1 and enabled edge throttling. Observing p95 for 10m — reporting back in 15m."

Escalation matrix (roles + contact cadence)
- 0–15 minutes: On-call engineer -> Bridge operator -> notify team channel and CS.
- 15–60 minutes: Escalation owner (tech lead) is paged.
- 60+ minutes: Eng manager and SRE lead notified; consider exec notification for Sev 1.

Game-day syllabus (45–90 minute exercises to validate the runloop)
- Goal: verify evidence collection, communication cadence, escalation fidelity, and rollback paths.
- Participants: 1 bridge operator, 2 on-call engineers (primary + backup), CS rep, 1 observations engineer.
- Scenarios (pick one per run):
  1) KV cache miss storm with rising p95.
  2) Model quality regression mid-rollout.
  3) Burst capacity exhaustion (GPU queue buildup).
- Success criteria: bridge established in <5 minutes, first status page posted in <20 minutes for Sev 2 equivalent, evidence artifacts captured, mitigation applied and validated, and a 30-minute retro scheduled.

Post-incident checklist and postmortem gates
- Postmortem timeline: draft due within 72 hours; peer review completed within 7 days; action items assigned and scheduled within 14 days.
- Minimum postmortem contents: impact timeline, root cause hypothesis, evidence, customer impact table, remediation plan, action owners, rehearsal/test plan for the fix.
- Severity to follow-up mapping: any Sev 1 or recurring Sev 2 -> mandatory blameless RCA session with Exec attendance.

SLA credit and billing note
- If incident meets SLA credit criteria (>=99.95% monthly API uptime violated for a billing tenant), Customer Success will initiate credit evaluation within 3 business days and coordinate legal/finance approval. Retain the incident evidence packet for audit.

Runbook hygiene and ownership
- Every on-call rotation should review and mark primary runbooks as "verified" after a game-day or production incident. The team runbook owner must update mitigation steps and tactics within 10 business days of the incident.

Appendix: quick commands and snippets
- List running runtime pods by CPU usage:
  kubectl top pods -n runtime | sort -k2 -nr | head -n 20
- Pull 10 slow traces from the observability backend (example):
  curl -G "https://obs-collector.internal/traces" --data-urlencode "service=redwood-runtime" --data-urlencode "min_duration_ms=200" | jq '.traces | .[:10]'

References and links
- Incident evidence template: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/incident-evidence-chain-and-forensic-runbook-2025
- Postmortem rubric and timeline: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/post-incident-learning-codex-handoff-and-synthesis-2025
